ABRAHAM.name: Abraham
ABRAHAM.desc: Abraham, a tall, upright old man who looks about eighty and is still strong, with warm brown, deeply weathered and lined skin, thick wavy white hair reaching his collar, a full white beard, white eyebrows, a strong straight nose and steady, thoughtful dark eyes, wearing an ankle-length long-sleeved tunic of undyed cream wool with a brown leather belt and a deep russet-red wool mantle draped over his left shoulder, and simple leather sandals

segs.text: Now Abraham had taken another wife, named Keturah,
and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were the Asshurites, the Letushites, and the Leummites.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were descendants of Keturah.
Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac.
But while he was still alive, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east.
Abraham lived a total of 175 years.
And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite.
This was the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites. Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah.
After Abraham’s death, God blessed his son Isaac, who lived near Beer-lahai-roi.
This is the account of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael in the order of their birth: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These were the sons of Ishmael, and these were their names by their villages and encampments—twelve princes of their tribes.
Ishmael lived a total of 137 years. Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
Ishmael’s descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur. And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers.
This is the account of Abraham’s son Isaac. Abraham became the father of Isaac,
and Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean.
Later, Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.
But the children inside her struggled with each other, and she said,
“Why is this happening to me?”
So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD,
and He declared to her:
“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”
When her time came to give birth, there were indeed twins in her womb.
The first one came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau.
After this, his brother came out grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born.
When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home.
Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob.
One day, while Jacob was cooking some stew, Esau came in from the field and was famished.
He said to Jacob,
“Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.”
(That is why he was also called Edom.)
“First sell me your birthright,”
Jacob replied.
“Look,”
said Esau,
“I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?”
“Swear to me first,”
Jacob said. So Esau swore to Jacob and sold him the birthright.
Then Jacob gave some bread and lentil stew to Esau, who ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham’s time. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar.
The LORD appeared to Isaac and said,
“Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you.
Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands, and through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.”
So Isaac settled in Gerar.
But when the men of that place asked about his wife, he said,
“She is my sister.”
For he was afraid to say,
“She is my wife,”
since he thought to himself,
“The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.”
When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech sent for Isaac and said,
“So she is really your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?”
Isaac replied,
“Because I thought I might die on account of her.”
“What is this you have done to us?”
asked Abimelech.
“One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.”
So Abimelech warned all the people, saying,
“Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”
Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him,
and he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.
He owned so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines envied him.
So the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
Then Abimelech said to Isaac,
“Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.”
So Isaac left that place and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.

Isaac reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham died. And he gave these wells the same names his father had given them.
Then Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen and said,
“The water is ours!”
So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him.
Then they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.
He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said,
“At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”
From there Isaac went up to Beersheba,
and that night the LORD appeared to him and said,
“I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.”
So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and he pitched his tent there. His servants also dug a well there.
Later, Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
“Why have you come to me?”
Isaac asked them.
“You hated me and sent me away.”
“We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,”
they replied.
“We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you. Let us make a covenant with you
that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you but have done only good to you, sending you on your way in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD.”
So Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
And they got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
On that same day, Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug.
“We have found water!”
they told him.
So he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba.
When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah: in {EASTLAND}, a deep-brown-skinned man of about thirty-five with a black beard, in a knee-length dull-green wool tunic, sits on a flat rock, and his five sons, boys between four and fourteen in short wool tunics of cream and brown, sit in a half circle on the ground in front of him, listening to him. Exactly one man and five boys: count the boys, five. A few goats graze far behind. No tents, no buildings. Medium wide view.

All these were descendants of Keturah: at the door of {TENT}, in evening light, {KETURAH}, sits on a woven rug with a small grandchild asleep in her lap, and beside her sits {ABRAHAM}, looking out past the camp, where a few young men and children of the household are small figures among the oaks. {NOHALO}. Medium view.

Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac: on a hillside above {CAMP}, with big flocks of sheep and goats, brown cattle and a few camels on the slopes below, {ABRAHAM}, on the left, lays his right hand on the shoulder of {ISAAC}, on the right, and with his other arm sweeps across the whole camp and all the flocks below. {TWOMEN}: one white-haired old man in a red mantle and one dark-haired bearded man of forty. {NOHALO}. Wide view.

While he was still alive, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines: in front of {TENT}, {ABRAHAM}, stands on the left and places a leather bag heavy with silver into the open hands of a deep-brown-skinned young man with a short black beard in a brown wool tunic; behind that young man two of his brothers, in grey and dull-green wool tunics, wait their turn, and beside them stand two laden grey donkeys and a few sheep. Exactly four men: one white-haired old man and three young men. {NOHALO}. Medium wide view.

And sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east: in the foreground on the left, seen from behind, {ABRAHAM}, stands on a rise with one hand lifted in farewell. Far below and beyond him, six young men seen from behind walk away from us in a line with laden donkeys, a few camels and small flocks, going out into {EASTLAND}, toward the pale light of the rising sun. The old man is seen only from behind. No tents, no buildings. Very wide view.

Abraham lived a total of 175 years: {INTENT}. A close view from the chest up of {ABRAHAM}, very old now, sitting propped against cushions, his lined face calm and his eyes looking far away, one weathered hand resting on a wooden staff. Behind him are only the dark tent cloth and a wooden pole. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. Close view.

At a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented: {NIGHTTENT}. {ABRAHAM}, lies on his back on the sleeping mat under a wool blanket, his eyes closed and his face peaceful, his hands folded on his chest. Beside the mat kneels {ISAAC_ELDER}, holding his father's hand in both of his, his head bowed. {TWOMEN}: one white-haired old man lying down and one grey-haired man kneeling. {NOHALO}. Medium view from the side.

And was gathered to his people: {NIGHTTENT}. The small clay oil lamp stands on the rug beside an empty sleeping mat and a wooden staff that leans against the tent pole; its single flame burns low. Through the open door flap is seen {STARS}. {NOPEOPLE}. Medium view, quiet and still.

His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him: at the edge of {MACHFIELD}, in grey early-morning light, two brothers stand face to face. On the left is {ISAAC_ELDER}, and on the right is {ISHMAEL_OLD}. They grip each other's right forearm, their faces grave. {TWOMEN}: one grey-haired man in a cream tunic with a dark-brown mantle and one grey-haired desert man in a sand-coloured cloak with a green sash. {NOTENTS}. Medium view in side view.

In the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite: a small procession crosses {MACHFIELD}, in side view from left to right, toward {CAVE}, which is seen at the far right. Four men of the household in plain knee-length tunics of undyed cream, brown and grey wool carry on their shoulders {BIER}. Close behind the bier walk two men side by side, their heads bowed: {ISAAC_ELDER}, and {ISHMAEL_OLD}. No one has white hair and no living person wears a red mantle. {NOTENTS}. Wide view.

{EMPTY}. This was the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites: a wide, quiet view over {MACHFIELD}, with {CAVE}, small at its far end, in soft golden late-afternoon light, and the low boundary wall of field stones running all around the field. No town, no tents, no animals. Wide view.

Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah: inside a dark natural limestone cave, two still shapes lie side by side on two low natural ledges of rock, each wrapped from head to foot in plain undyed cream linen: over the farther one lies a faded, dusty indigo-blue wool shawl, and over the nearer one a deep russet-red wool mantle. No faces, no hands and no skin are seen. One small clay oil lamp with a single flame stands on the rock floor between them and lights the rough rock walls. {NOPEOPLE}: no living person. No masonry, no carving. Medium view.

After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac, who lived near Beer-lahai-roi: beside {WELL}, in {NEGEV}, in the clear light of early morning, {ISAAC_ELDER}, stands with one hand resting on the stones of the well and his face lifted, while soft golden-white light falls on him from above the frame; behind him, a little way off, lies {NEGEVCAMP}, with many sheep and goats around it. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. Medium wide view.

This is the account of Abraham's son Ishmael: on a ridge of bare red-brown desert rock at sunset, {ISHMAEL_OLD}, stands in three-quarter view looking out over a vast, empty desert of sand and stone, leaning on {BOW}, held upright like a staff, the wind pulling at his cloak. {ONE}. No tents, no animals, no buildings. Medium wide view.

{MEMORY}. Whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham: at the door of a black goat-hair tent sits a slender young Egyptian woman of about twenty-five with reddish-brown skin, dark almond-shaped eyes and straight black hair cut level at the shoulders with a straight fringe, in a long-sleeved servant's dress of plain sand-brown wool with a faded green sash, holding in her arms {BABY}, with reddish-brown skin, and looking down at him. Exactly one woman and one baby. {NOHALO}. Medium close view.

These are the names of the sons of Ishmael in the order of their birth: in front of {DESERTCAMP}, {ISHMAEL_OLD}, stands on the left with one hand on the shoulder of his firstborn, a tall desert tribesman of about forty-five with a black beard and a rust-red sash, who stands beside him; both look toward a group of younger men gathered at the right of the picture, some of the {ISHMAELITES}. {NOHORSES}. No buildings. Medium wide view.

Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam: four desert tribesmen stand side by side on bare tawny ground, facing us, from the oldest on the left to the youngest on the right: {ISHMAELITES}; the first has a black beard and a rust-red sash, the second a green sash and a herdsman's staff, the third a blue sash, the fourth is a beardless youth. Exactly four men: count them, four. Behind them only desert and sky. No tents, no animals. Medium wide view.

Mishma, Dumah, Massa: three desert tribesmen, brothers, sit on the ground around a small evening campfire in bare desert, {ISHMAELITES}; one mends a leather strap, one stirs a small pot, one looks up at the first stars. Exactly three men: count them, three. Two camels kneel in the shadows behind them. No tents, no buildings. Medium view.

Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah: five desert tribesmen walk in single file in side view from left to right along the crest of a pale sand ridge at dawn, each leading one laden tan one-humped camel by a rope: {ISHMAELITES}. Exactly five men and five camels: count them, five. No tents, no buildings. Wide view.

{EMPTY}. These were their names by their villages and encampments: seen from a height in clear morning light, a broad desert valley holds, on the near side, a small village of low, flat-roofed huts of dry stone round a well with a few date palms, and, farther off, two encampments of small black goat-hair tents, tiny in the distance, with tiny flocks like scattered dots. No towers, no walls round the village, no flags. Very wide view from a height.

Twelve princes of their tribes: twelve desert chieftains stand in two straight rows facing us on bare tawny ground, six men in the front row and six men in the back row standing on a low bank just behind them, so that every one of the twelve faces is seen: {ISHMAELITES}, each holding a plain wooden staff upright in his right hand. Exactly twelve men in all, no more and no fewer: six in front and six behind, count them, twelve. No tents, no animals, no banners. Wide view.

Ishmael lived a total of 137 years: at the door of a black goat-hair tent in the desert, in the last red light of evening, {ISHMAEL_OLD}, sits on a rug with {BOW}, laid unstrung across his knees, his weathered hands resting on it, looking toward the sinking light. {ONE}. No animals, no buildings. Medium view.

Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people: at the door of a black goat-hair tent in the desert at night, under {STARS}, an unstrung wooden bow and a leather quiver lean against the tent pole beside an empty rug, and a small fire has burned down to red embers. {NOPEOPLE}. Medium view, quiet and still.

{EMPTY}. Ishmael's descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur: a vast desert seen from a high cliff in the clear light of morning: ridges of bare red-brown rock, pale gravel plains and long tawny dunes running away to a far hazy horizon, with small clusters of black tents scattered here and there across it, tiny in the distance. No buildings, no river, no palm groves. Very wide view from a height.

And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers: on opposite banks of a dry desert gully two bands of men stand facing each other in side view. On the left bank four desert tribesmen, {ISHMAELITES}, with staffs and unstrung bows held at their sides; on the right bank four herdsmen in brown and grey wool tunics with staffs. The two bands glare at each other across the empty gully; one man on each side points an accusing arm at the other side. Exactly eight men. {NOBLOWS}. No one draws a bow and no arrow flies. Wide view.

{MEMORY}. This is the account of Abraham's son Isaac. Abraham became the father of Isaac: in front of a black goat-hair tent, {ABRAHAM}, laughing with joy, lifts up in both hands {BABY}, with warm brown skin, and looks up into the child's face. Exactly one old man and one baby. {NOHALO}. Medium close view.

Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah: in front of {TENT}, in {NEGEV}, in golden evening light, {ISAAC}, on the left and {REBEKAH}, on the right stand face to face, and he holds both her hands in his; she looks up at him, her face uncovered, smiling. {TWO}: one man and one young woman. {NOHALO}. No animals. Medium view in side view.

{MEMORY}. {EMPTY}. The daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean: far away across a wide green plain, a small walled town of tan mud brick with flat roofs stands on a low mound beside a broad, slow river, with a round stone-lined well outside its gate. No domes, no arches, no towers with pointed roofs, no tents, no travellers. Very wide view.

Because she was barren: at the edge of {NEGEVCAMP}, {REBEKAH}, stands alone in the foreground at the left holding an empty clay water jar against her hip, and watches with a quiet, sad face two women of the camp in plain wool dresses and head shawls who sit far off at the right with small children playing round them. Her arms hold no child. {NOHALO}. Medium wide view.

Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife: on a stony rise in {NEGEV}, in the grey-blue light before dawn, {ISAAC}, kneels alone in side view with both open hands lifted in front of him and his face raised to the sky. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NEGEVBG}. No tents. Medium view.

And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived: {INTENT}. {REBEKAH_MATRON}, sits on a cushion in the soft light from the door, both hands laid on the gentle roundness of her belly under her dress, looking down with a wondering smile, while a warm golden-white light falls on her from above. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. Medium view.

But the children inside her struggled with each other: {NIGHTTENT}. {REBEKAH_MATRON}, heavily pregnant under her dress, half sits up on her sleeping mat, one hand pressed to the side of her great belly and the other braced on the rugs, her brows drawn in pain and alarm. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. Medium view.

So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD: at first light in {NEGEV}, {REBEKAH_MATRON}, heavily pregnant, walks alone in side view from left to right up a stony path away from the black tents far behind her at the left, one hand under her belly and the other holding her head scarf against the wind, her face lifted toward the brightening sky ahead. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. No animals. Wide view.

And He declared to her: on a stony hilltop in {NEGEV}, {REBEKAH_MATRON}, heavily pregnant, kneels with her hands open on her knees and her face lifted, and over her pours {GLORY}. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. Medium wide view from a little below.

{VISION}. Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated: from one single point in the foreground two great crowds of people walk away in two different directions, one multitude streaming away toward the upper left and the other streaming away toward the upper right, with a widening empty space of bare ground between them, so that the two crowds form a great letter V seen from above. No banners, no weapons, no buildings. Wide view from a height.

{VISION}. One people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger: two silhouettes of men stand facing each other in side view against the amber glow. The one on the left is taller and broader, with a shaggy head of hair, and he bows low from the waist with his head down; the one on the right is smaller and slighter and stands upright. Exactly two silhouettes, without faces. No weapons, no crowns, no thrones. Medium wide view.

When her time came to give birth: outside {TENT}, at night in {NEGEV}, warm lamplight glows through the cloth of the closed tent. Two serving women in plain wool dresses and head shawls hurry toward the closed door flap, one carrying a clay basin of water and one a bundle of folded cloths. A few paces from the tent, {ISAAC_ELDER}, stands waiting, his hands clasped, looking at the tent. The door flap is closed: nothing inside the tent is seen. Above is {STARS}. Medium wide view.

There were indeed twins in her womb: {NIGHTTENT}. A grey-haired midwife in a plain brown wool dress and head shawl kneels on the rugs, seen from the side, and holds in her two arms two newborn babies at once, each wrapped in undyed cream wool swaddling cloth, looking from one small face to the other in astonishment: the baby in her left arm has ruddy red skin and thick dark-red hair, and the baby in her right arm has smooth warm brown skin and a little dark-brown hair. Exactly one woman and two wrapped babies. Medium close view.

The first one came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau: {NIGHTTENT}. A very close view of {REDBABY}, lying in the weathered hands of a midwife, lit by the lamp. Only the baby and the woman's hands and forearms are seen. One baby only. Close view.

After this, his brother came out grasping Esau's heel: a very close view, lit by warm lamplight, of two newborn babies lying side by side on a cream wool blanket, both wrapped in undyed cream wool swaddling cloth. From the wrapping of the baby on the right one tiny, smooth, brown hand reaches out and holds tightly on to the small ruddy heel of the baby on the left, whose one little foot, downy with fine dark-red hair, sticks out of its cloth. The tiny hand gripping the tiny heel is in the middle of the picture. Only the two babies, no adults. Close view.

So he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born: {INTENT}. {ISAAC_ELDER}, sits on the rugs holding one wrapped newborn baby in the crook of each arm and looking down at them with quiet joy: in his right arm {REDBABY}; in his left arm {SMOOTHBABY}. Exactly one man and two babies. {NOHALO}. Medium close view.

When the boys grew up: on pale stony ground at the edge of a camp of black tents in {NEGEV}, two twin brothers who do not look alike stand side by side facing us. On the left is {BOYESAU}, holding a small toy bow of bent wood. On the right is {BOYJACOB}, holding a young lamb in his arms. Exactly two boys, no one else. Medium view.

Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field: in open, hilly country of dry grass, rock and thorn scrub in early morning light, {ESAU}, with a leather quiver on his back, crouches in side view behind a boulder at the left, holding {BOW}, low in his left hand with one arrow set on the string, pointing at the ground, and watches a gazelle that grazes far off at the right. {ONE}. No tents, no buildings. Wide view.

While Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home: among the black goat-hair tents of a camp in {NEGEV}, in calm afternoon light, {JACOB}, sits on a rug at the door of {TENT}, mending a leather water skin with a bone needle and cord, while a few sheep and goats lie in the shade beside him. {ONE}. No bow, no weapons. Medium view.

Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau: {INTENT}. On the left {ISAAC_ELDER}, sits on a cushion eating with relish from a clay bowl of roasted meat in his lap. On the right, facing him, {ESAU}, kneels on one knee, having just set the bowl before him, and watches his father eat with a proud grin. The father smiles warmly at him. {TWOMEN}: one grey-haired man in a cream tunic and one big red-haired man in a goatskin cape. Medium view.

But Rebekah loved Jacob: at the door of {TENT}, in soft morning light, {REBEKAH_MATRON}, on the left and {JACOB}, on the right sit side by side at a small upright wooden weaving frame; she rests one hand fondly on his shoulder and smiles at him as he holds a ball of wool yarn for her. {TWO}: one woman and one man. No animals. Medium view.

One day, while Jacob was cooking some stew: {COOKPLACE}, {JACOB}, crouches in side view beside {POT}, and stirs it with a long wooden spoon. The stew in the pot is deep red. {ONE}. {COOKBG}. Medium view.

Esau came in from the field and was famished: at the edge of a camp in {NEGEV}, in late-afternoon light, {ESAU}, with a leather quiver on his back, trudges toward us out of the open country, dusty and spent, his shoulders sagging, dragging {BOW}, in one hand so that its tip trails on the ground; his other hand is empty: he has caught nothing. One black tent stands far behind him at the side. {ONE}. No game, no animals. Medium wide view.

Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished: {COOKPLACE}. In the middle stands {POT}. On the left {ESAU}, has dropped to his knees in the dust and points with one hairy hand at the pot, his mouth open, his eyes fixed on the stew. On the right, on the other side of the pot, {JACOB}, crouches with the long wooden spoon in his hand and looks at him steadily. {TWOMEN}: one big red-haired man and one lean dark-haired man. {COOKBG}. Medium view in side view.

That red stew (that is why he was also called Edom): a very close view straight down into a round, soot-blackened clay cooking pot full of thick, steaming, deep-red lentil stew, with a long wooden spoon resting in it, and small flames licking round the three stones under the pot at the edges of the picture. The stew is unmistakably red. {NOPEOPLE}: no hands, no faces. Very close view from above.

First sell me your birthright: {COOKPLACE}. A close view from the chest up of {JACOB}, speaking quietly, his eyes sharp and steady on someone just outside the left of the picture, holding a wooden spoon upright in one hand like a man naming his price. {ONE}. Behind him are only the dark tent cloth and far bare hills. Close view.

Look, I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me? {COOKPLACE}. A close view from the chest up of {ESAU}, dusty and hollow-eyed with hunger, throwing up one hairy open hand in careless impatience as he speaks to someone just outside the right of the picture. {ONE}. Behind him are only pale stony ground and far bare hills. Close view.

Swear to me first: {COOKPLACE}. {JACOB}, stands beside {POT}, holding one hand flat above the pot as if to keep it back, and lifts the first finger of his other hand, his face firm, looking toward someone just outside the left of the picture. {ONE}. {COOKBG}. Medium view.

So Esau swore to Jacob and sold him the birthright: {COOKPLACE}. On the left {ESAU}, kneeling in the dust, raises his right hand open beside his shoulder, swearing an oath, his eyes not on his brother but on the pot. On the right {JACOB}, stands facing him and watches the raised hand closely. Between them stands {POT}. {TWOMEN}: one big red-haired man kneeling and one lean dark-haired man standing. {COOKBG}. Medium view in side view.

Then Jacob gave some bread and lentil stew to Esau: {COOKPLACE}. On the right {JACOB}, holds out with both hands a clay bowl of deep-red lentil stew with a round flat loaf of bread laid across its rim. On the left {ESAU}, kneeling, reaches up for it eagerly with both hairy hands. {TWOMEN}: one big red-haired man kneeling and one lean dark-haired man standing. {COOKBG}. Medium view in side view.

Who ate and drank: {COOKPLACE}. {ESAU}, sits cross-legged on the ground, hunched over a clay bowl of deep-red lentil stew held close under his chin, scooping the stew up with a torn piece of flat bread, a clay cup standing by his knee. {ONE}. {COOKBG}. Medium close view.

And then got up and went away: seen from behind, {ESAU}, with a leather quiver on his back and {BOW}, in his hand, walks away from us across pale stony ground toward the open country, not looking back. In the foreground at the right, {JACOB}, stands beside a black tent with an empty clay bowl in his hands and watches him go. The red-haired man is seen only from behind. {TWOMEN}. No animals, no buildings. Wide view.

Thus Esau despised his birthright: a very close view of an empty clay bowl lying tipped on its side on pale stony ground, with a smear of deep-red stew drying inside it and a few crumbs of bread beside it, in the long low light of evening, the long shadow of a tent pole falling across it. {NOPEOPLE}: no hands, no faces. Very close view.

{EMPTY}. Now there was another famine in the land: {FAMINE}. In the foreground lie a cracked, empty clay water jar and the dry stalks of a failed barley field. No animals, no bones, no bodies, no tents, no buildings. Wide view.

{MEMORY}. Subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham's time: across {FAMINE}, seen in side view from far off, {ABRAHAM}, walks from left to right, leaning on a staff, leading one laden grey donkey, with a few small figures of his household and thin sheep trailing behind him. All of them are small in a wide, empty land. No camels, no buildings. Very wide view.

And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar: on a dusty road in dry grassland, seen from behind, {ISAAC_ELDER}, and beside him {REBEKAH_MATRON}, walk away from us at the head of a small household with laden grey donkeys and thin sheep, toward {GERAR}, which stands ahead of them in the middle distance. The two are seen from behind, walking away from us. {NOHORSES}. No tents. Wide view.

The LORD appeared to Isaac: on dry grassland at dusk, {ISAAC_ELDER}, walking alone, has stopped short and half raised one arm before his face, as in front of him pours {GLORY}, lighting the grass around his feet. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. {NOTOWN}. Medium wide view.

{EMPTY}. Do not go down to Egypt: a dusty caravan road runs away from us southward across a dry, stony desert plain toward a far horizon, where a thin line of green and a pale glint of water lie under the haze. In the foreground the road forks, and the branch that leads on toward the far green line is quite empty: no footprints on it, no travellers. No pyramids, no buildings, no palm trees nearby. Very wide view.

Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you: on dry grassland at dusk, a close view from the chest up of {ISAAC_ELDER}, kneeling, his face lifted and lit from above by warm golden-white light, his lips parted in awe, his hands open in front of him. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. Behind him are only dim grassland and darkening sky. Close view.

{EMPTY}. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring: seen from a high hill in the golden light of evening, land beyond land spreads out to the far horizon: dry grassland with a winding dry stream bed in front, then green limestone hills with olive trees, then far blue mountains, and to one side a pale line of sea. No towns, no tents, no roads. Very wide view from a height.

{MEMORY}. I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham: on a hilltop at night, seen from behind and a little below, {ABRAHAM}, stands alone with his head tilted back, looking up into {STARS}. He is seen only from behind, a dark figure against the stars. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. No tents. Wide view.

{EMPTY}. I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky: {STARS}, filling almost the whole picture, above a low, dark line of grassland at the very bottom edge. {NOPEOPLE}. Very wide view, looking up.

{VISION}. And I will give them all these lands: a great multitude of people, families with children and flocks, spreads out over rolling hills and valleys as far as can be seen, pitching tents and tilling fields, all of them small faceless silhouettes against the amber glow. No banners, no weapons, no city walls. Very wide view from a height.

{VISION}. Through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed: many separate streams of people, in the differing dress of many lands, some in long robes, some in short kilts, some in cloaks and tall caps, walk in from every edge of the picture toward one clear, soft, golden-white light that rises at the centre of the horizon, their dark faceless figures edged with its light. {NOLIGHTFIG}. No banners, no weapons, no buildings. Very wide view.

{MEMORY}. Because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes and My laws: on a hilltop in {CANAAN}, {ABRAHAM}, kneels in side view before {ALTAR}, his head bowed and his open hands lifted, while soft golden-white light falls on him from above the frame. {NOFIRE}. {ONE}. {NOHALO}. {NOLIGHTFIG}. No tents. Medium wide view.

So Isaac settled in Gerar: outside the wall of {GERAR}, {ISAAC_ELDER}, in the foreground, drives a wooden tent peg into the ground with a stone, kneeling beside a half-pitched tent of black goat-hair cloth, while two men of his household in plain wool tunics raise the tent poles behind him. Exactly three men. {NOHORSES}. Medium wide view.

When the men of that place asked about his wife: {GERARSTREET}. In the middle {ISAAC_ELDER}, stands facing three {GERARMEN}, who stand at the right; the foremost of them points past Isaac's shoulder with a questioning look at {REBEKAH_MATRON}, who stands a few paces behind Isaac at the left, holding a clay water jar, her eyes lowered. Exactly five people: Isaac, one woman and three men of Gerar. {NOBLOWS}. Medium wide view.

He said, She is my sister: {GERARSTREET}. A close view from the chest up of {ISAAC_ELDER}, answering with a strained, uneasy smile, his eyes sliding aside, one open hand gesturing back over his shoulder. {ONE}. Behind him is only a plain tan mud-brick wall. Close view.

For he was afraid to say, She is my wife, since he thought to himself, The men of this place will kill me: {GERARSTREET}. {ISAAC_ELDER}, walks toward us along the street with his head down and his shoulders hunched, glancing fearfully sideways, while behind him four {GERARMEN}, stand in a doorway and watch him go with hard, measuring eyes. Exactly five men. {NOBLOWS}. No weapons in any hand. Medium view.

On account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful: beside a round stone well in a small open square of the town of Gerar, among plain tan mud-brick houses, a close view from the waist up of {REBEKAH_MATRON}, lifting a clay water jar to her shoulder, her face uncovered and lovely in the clear morning light; far behind her, small and out of focus, two townsmen have turned their heads to look at her. {NOHALO}. No domes, no arches, no columns. Medium close view.

{EMPTY}. When Isaac had been there a long time: {GERAR}, seen from the grassland in the gold of a summer evening, and beside its wall a settled camp of black goat-hair tents with a small fenced vegetable plot, a worn footpath to the gate and well-grown young fig trees beside the tents. No people near, no horses, no flags. Wide view.

Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window: seen from outside and a little below, an upper window of the king's house, a plain square opening in a thick whitewashed mud-brick wall. In it {ABIMELECH_OLD}, seen from the chest up, leans with both hands on the sill and looks down toward something below and to the left of the picture, his heavy eyebrows raised in surprise. {ONE}. card_notes: Every spoken word is Scripture: Genesis 25:1–26:35, complete.
notes: Text: Genesis 25:1-34 and 26:1-35 in full, no verses skipped or abridged (69 verses). Speakers: N narrator, R Rebekah (25:22), G the LORD (25:23, 26:2-5, 26:24; the voice used for God since Genesis 1), E Esau (25:30, 25:32), J Jacob (25:31, 25:33), I Isaac (26:7, 26:9, 26:22, 26:27; Isaac's voice from s02e02d lowered one semitone for his age, a default that can be changed in 'voices'), K Abimelech (26:9-11, 26:16, and 26:28-29, which the text gives to 'they', the king with Ahuzzath and Phicol, spoken here by the king alone), H the herdsmen of Gerar (26:20), V Isaac's servants (26:32). The words Isaac says and thinks in 26:7 are in his own voice; Abimelech's quotation of him in 26:9 stays in the king's voice. The local BSB snapshot was read verse by verse for both chapters; no slips found.

Still tags: T = from the text, I = inferred, D = dramatized. REF = character reference sheet (not used in the film, no clip). Still 'verses' are chapter:verse; still ids are A (chapter 25) or B (chapter 26), the verse number and a letter (B07c = third picture of 26:7); clips are V-<still id>.

Order: the pictures follow the text's order, not a reconstructed chronology. By the text's own numbers (21:5, 25:7, 25:26) Abraham dies when the twins are fifteen, but the text tells his death first, and so does the film. Chapter 26 names no children; none are shown in Gerar, and whether the stay there came before or after the twins' birth is not decided on screen.

Life stages and sheets. Abraham uses refs/REF-ABRAHAM.jpg (s02e01e) with its text word for word; at 175 he is the same man, only seated or lying. Isaac at forty (25:5, 25:20-21) uses refs/REF-ISAAC.jpg and Rebekah as a bride (25:20, 25:21a) refs/REF-REBEKAH.jpg, both from s02e02f, text word for word. New in this unit: refs/REF-ISAAC-ELDER.jpg (key ISAAC_ELDER), Isaac from sixty onward (25:26; he is seventy-five at the burial of 25:9 and a hundred at 26:34), a grey-haired man who looks about sixty, derived from REF-ISAAC, same clothes; refs/REF-REBEKAH-MATRON.jpg (key REBEKAH_MATRON), Rebekah about twenty years after her marriage and later, a woman of about forty who is still 'so beautiful' (26:7), derived from REF-REBEKAH, same dress with long sleeves. Genesis 27 needs Isaac old and blind (27:1): derive that sheet from REF-ISAAC-ELDER.

Esau and Jacob (new sheets refs/REF-ESAU.jpg and refs/REF-JACOB.jpg, keys ESAU and JACOB). T: Esau was born red and hairy all over (25:25), is a hunter and a man of the field (25:27), and Jacob is a quiet man of the tents (25:27) and a smooth man (27:11). I: everything else, namely their looking about thirty (one sheet serves from the stew to Esau's marriage at forty and can serve Genesis 27-28), Esau's dark-red hair and beard (the text says he came out red, not that his hair was red), his goatskin cape and quiver, Jacob's dark-brown hair and sand-yellow tunic. They are twins who do not look alike. Newborns and ten-year-olds are description blocks (REDBABY, SMOOTHBABY, BOYESAU, BOYJACOB).

Ishmael (new sheet refs/REF-ISHMAEL-OLD.jpg, key ISHMAEL_OLD, derived from the boy's sheet refs/REF-ISHMAEL.jpg): by the text's numbers he is eighty-nine at Abraham's burial and dies at 137; he is painted as an old desert man who looks about seventy. s02e02c designs him at about twenty-five (REF-ISHMAEL-MAN), which was not yet generated when this unit was written. A12b recalls Hagar with the infant Ishmael (description follows the HAGAR text of s02e01d, no sheet attached).

Abimelech of Genesis 26. Whether he is the Abimelech of Genesis 20-21 grown very old, or a later king of the same name or title, is disputed and the text does not say; likewise Phicol. The picture does not decide: the king (new sheet refs/REF-ABIMELECH-OLD.jpg, key ABIMELECH_OLD) has the build, square face, heavy brows and royal dress described for Abimelech in s02e02b, word for word, but iron-grey hair and beard and the look of a man of about seventy, so he can be taken as the same man in old age or as a son who resembles him. The sheet is not derived from refs/REF-ABIMELECH.jpg only because that sheet did not exist yet. Phicol (block PHICOL: the s02e02c description with white hair and without the scar) and Ahuzzath (block AHUZZATH, all I) have no sheets. 'Philistines' are dressed as the men of Gerar of s02e02b (GERARMEN): no Aegean or feathered-headdress dress, and whether the name is a later one for the people of the region is not decided on screen.

25:1-6. 'Abraham had taken another wife': when he took Keturah (before or after Sarah's death) is disputed; A01a shows only the two together, with the aged Abraham, and Sarah is not in the picture. Keturah (block KETURAH) and her sons (SIXSONS) are I in every detail. A03a, A03b, A04a picture the names of 25:3-4 as fathers with sons and as tent clusters (I); no people or place known from other sources is identified. 25:6 'the sons of his concubines': three of Keturah's sons receive gifts (A06a) and six leave (A06b); Ishmael, sent away in Genesis 21, is not among them. A04b (Keturah with a grandchild) is I.

25:7-10. Abraham's death is a quiet deathbed (A08a); that Isaac is beside him is I. 'Gathered to his people' is an empty mat and a lamp going out (A08b, D). A09a (the brothers meeting at the field) is I: the text says only that both buried him. The body is a wrapped shape on a bier with his red mantle laid over it (no face). A10b shows two wrapped shapes in the cave, Sarah's with her faded blue shawl as in s02e02e. The blocks MACHFIELD, CAVE and BIER follow s02e02e.

25:11 and after: Isaac's home is a camp in the Negev by a stone-ringed well (blocks NEGEVCAMP, WELL from s02e02f; Beer-lahai-roi is not otherwise marked). God's blessing is light from above, never a figure.

25:12-18. The twelve sons are shown in the text's groups of names (A13b four, A14a three, A15a five) and once together (A16b, exactly twelve); the firstborn Nebaioth is singled out in A13a. Dress is that of desert herdsmen (block ISHMAELITES, I). 'Villages and encampments' (A16a) are dry-stone huts and tents (I). 'From Havilah to Shur' is a desert seen from a height; no place is marked. 25:18b follows the BSB main text, 'they lived in hostility toward all their brothers' (other renderings: 'he settled over against all his kinsmen'): two bands glare across a gully, and no blow or weapon in use is shown (A18b).

25:21-26. Rebekah's barrenness (A21a) and Isaac's prayer (A21b) are shown apart; the twenty years between marriage and birth (25:20, 25:26) are marked only by the change from the young to the older sheet. 25:22 'went to inquire of the LORD': where and how is not said; she walks out alone and kneels on a hilltop, and the answer is light and a voice (A22b, A23a; no priest, altar or prophet is shown). The oracle is two faceless visions (A23b, A23c); no nation is named or marked. The birth itself is not shown: a closed lamplit tent (A24a), then the wrapped newborns (A24b-A26b). 'Covered with hair like a fur coat' is a ruddy baby with thick dark-red hair and downy cheeks and arm; 'grasping Esau's heel' is a small hand on a small heel, both babies wrapped (A26a).

25:27-34. A27a (the boys at ten, with a toy bow and a lamb) is I. Esau the hunter stalks a gazelle and no kill is shown (A27b). 25:28: Isaac eats game Esau has brought (A28a); Rebekah and Jacob at a weaving frame (A28b) is I. The stew is deep-red lentil stew (25:30 'red stew', 25:34 'lentil stew') in a clay pot outside a tent; Esau comes back empty-handed (I, from 'famished'). The oath is a raised right hand (I). The film adds no judgement on either brother beyond the text's own last sentence, which is spoken over the emptied bowl (A34d).

26:1-6. The famine is bare cracked land with no dead animals or bodies. B01b recalls Abraham's famine of 12:10. The LORD's appearing (26:2, 26:24) is GLORY, light from above with no figure; 'do not go down to Egypt' is an empty road south with a far green line (B02b; no pyramids). The promises are landscape, stars and faceless visions (B03b-B04c); B04c shows the nations coming toward a formless light, and no nation or later event is identified. B03c, B05a and B24b recall Abraham (under the stars of 15:5, at an altar, walking in the light); they are memories of earlier scenes, tagged T for the words they sit under.

26:7-11. The men of Gerar ask about Rebekah in a street (I); Isaac's fear is pictured as men watching him (B07c), with no weapon and no threat acted on. 26:8 'caressing': the BSB word is shown as an embrace on a garden bench seen from the king's window, a hand on her cheek, both fully dressed, no kiss (B08c); the Hebrew word plays on Isaac's name ('laughing'), and she is laughing. Abimelech's window is an upper window of a mud-brick house (I). 26:10 is pictured only as a townsman looking after Rebekah in the street (B10b). 26:11: the king warns the people at the gate (I) and the townsmen draw back from the couple (B11b); no punishment is shown.

26:12-22. Sowing and a hundredfold harvest are barley (I). Wealth is silver rings, wool and grain jars (I; no coins). 26:15 and 26:18 are told in the text's order: the wells are filled (B15a, B15b), Isaac is sent away, then reopens them. The quarrels over Esek and Sitnah are shouting and pushing forward only: no blow, no drawn blade (blocks NOBLOWS, GHERDS, IHERDS). The names Esek, Sitnah, Rehoboth and Shibah are spoken, never written on screen. 26:19 'a well of fresh water' (literally living water) is water bubbling up in the bottom of a newly dug pit.

26:23-33. The altar at Beersheba is unhewn stones with no fire and no sacrifice, since the text names none (blocks ALTAR, NOFIRE from s02e01a). Abimelech, Ahuzzath and Phicol come on foot with no escort (I). The feast is bread, meat and dates (I). The oath is raised right hands and then a clasp of forearms, as in s02e02c (I: the text describes no rite). B29b recalls the sending away of 26:16 under the king's words 'sending you on your way in peace'; the film does not comment on the difference between his account and 26:27. 26:33 'to this day the name of the city is Beersheba': B33b shows a later small town grown up round the well (I); how this naming relates to Abraham's in 21:31 is not resolved.

26:34-35. Esau's wives Judith and Basemath (block WIVES) are I in every detail; they are dressed like the Hittites of s02e02e. How they 'brought grief' is not said and not shown: B34b shows only their arrival and the parents' faces, B35a the parents alone.
Narration is not generated in this unit; shots are laid at assembly.
